comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
In 2000 if you told me that a computer would generate a novel coherent sentence, let alone several paragraphs of grammatically correct English I would have called you a liar.


The dissociated-press algorithm was published in 1972. Don Mitchell's markov was the basis for Mark V. Shaney and similar works in the early 80s. Racter was available for home computers by 1985. The bidirectional integrated interactive-fiction environment Inform 6 was published in 1996.

I do think that there's an interesting nuance here which might be steering your thoughts. We didn't have a reliable way to parse English until about 2013, described here. Chatbots are usually not used for generating arbitrary text, but for generating text conditioned on some context ("prompt"), which in full generality implies that the bot ought to be able to parse the prompt to answer questions like "how many 'r' are in this sentence?" or "what is the main verb of this sentence?" In this sense, although our generative capabilities have been slowly increasing since the 1960s, it is only recently that we have been able to complete the loop which makes the ELIZA effect so potent by fooling the user into thinking that the bot understands English by both reading and writing English.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
whether Machines Can Think… is about as relevant as the question of whether Submarines Can Swim


LLMs can do useful things processing text, but the way they do it is substantially different from how humans think. This isn't to say it's always worse, but the similarities can be superficial and deceptive, and the flaws can be surprising.

We have something that seems to be able to discuss quantum physics—in 17 languages simultaneously—but struggle to count letters in "strawberry" (due to architectural reasons). There are bunch of other less obvious systemic flaws.

More practically, LLM's ability to write correct-looking text is way ahead of getting its substance correct (they're language models, not world models). This is a trap for people - when we deal with other people saying dumb things, the quality of the content and its form are usually correlated. When you see "how is baby formed" you immediately know what to expect, but an LLM is able to improve the form even when it can't improve the substance, and say the same thing like "The origin of offspring is a conundrum". It bypasses people's heuristics and takes more effort to recognize when it's nonsense.

comments.author: stapelberg
comments.text:
See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functionalism_(philosophy_of_mind) for the larger technical term.

Quoting from that page’s Criticism → Chinese Room section:


In short, Searle describes a person who only speaks English who is in a room with only Chinese symbols in baskets and a rule book in English for moving the symbols around. The person is then ordered by people outside of the room to follow the rule book for sending certain symbols out of the room when given certain symbols. Further suppose that the people outside of the room are Chinese speakers and are communicating with the person inside via the Chinese symbols. According to Searle, it would be absurd to claim that the English speaker inside knows Chinese simply based on these syntactic processes. This thought experiment attempts to show that systems which operate merely on syntactic processes (inputs and outputs, based on algorithms) cannot realize any semantics (meaning) or intentionality (aboutness). Thus, Searle attacks the idea that thought can be equated with following a set of syntactic rules.


Personally, I don’t find this thought experiment particularly interesting or applicable. The “[…] ordered by people outside of the room to follow the rule book […]” is too mysterious: In an LLM, there are no people outside the room applying a rule book. The setup of this experiment doesn’t match the situation we’re in (or I don’t understand how the setup maps).

I find the “China Brain” section directly above the “Chinese Room” section more relevant:


Ned Block[18] argues against the functionalist proposal of multiple realizability, where hardware implementation is irrelevant because only the functional level is important. The "China brain" or "Chinese nation" thought experiment involves supposing that the entire nation of China systematically organizes itself to operate just like a brain, with each individual acting as a neuron. (The tremendous difference in speed of operation of each unit is not addressed.). According to functionalism, so long as the people are performing the proper functional roles, with the proper causal relations between inputs and outputs, the system will be a real mind, with mental states, consciousness, and so on. Ned Block contends that this scenario is implausible, suggesting that there must be a flaw in the functionalist thesis if it allows such a system to be considered a legitimate mind.


So in today’s world, we replace “Nation with lots of people” with “silicon”.

I think LLMs are best seen as philosophical zombies, meaning they lack the ability to feel in the human sense (→ no Phenomenal consciousness), but they do seem to exhibit Access consciousness and Self-consciousness.

So that means LLMs are not sentient and therefore not conscious.

And yet, I have successfully used LLMs hundreds of times to solve problems where I would have thought they require (human) reasoning skills. I stand corrected. Either the LLMs are reasoning, or the problem space of programming doesn’t require reasoning.

Functionalism appeals to me: It is compatible with what I am observing.

In comparison, Ned Block’s argument boils down to: “This scenario is implausible”, to which my response is: “Well, yeah, but I have seen it happen!”

comments.author: stapelberg

(Over the last few months, I was also deeply unsettled by how little people value determinism.)

LLMs can be run deterministically. Specifically, I have done so by setting the temperature/seed to 0, not quantizing the context window, not using batch inference.

I have done this with open-weight local models (e.g. Ministral, Qwen, etc.) while developing a self-hosted spam filter and it was very useful. Before (non-deterministic inference), the spam/ham scores changed with every attempt, but after, they stayed perfectly identical across runs.

So If non-determinism is what prevents you from getting value out of LLMs, just know that you can get value out of LLMs when running them deterministically.

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
(Not directly about the linked article, but about Generative AI: Search., which is linked from it.)


I don't know how this will evolve, but I think it will follow the classic curve we've seen with search engines and forums and code forges: It's free at first, then the (new) owners try to make money, they make it terrible, a new service springs up, everyone moves there, and the cycle repeats.


That cycle worked because the entry barriers were low enough that a new service could spring up. A scrappy team could start a new forum, a new code forge, a new search engine. The incumbent's failure created a gap; competition could fill it.

Training a competitive LLM doesn't work like that. The training data—much of it scraped from the open web and from F/OSS repositories—already exists inside a handful of companies. Reproducing it requires capital at a scale that forecloses the kind of grassroots competition the cycle depended on. When the commons that trained the models is enclosed into proprietary weights, there's no guarantee anyone gets to build the “better service” that comes next. I've written more on this here.
